name: Uma Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write and produce music from a little studio in the back room of our flat. Mornings are library music, which is background tracks that video makers and podcasts license, and jingles when an agency sends a brief. I use AI tools all day, to split stems, rough out a mix or test ten drum grooves in a minute. Two nights a week I rehearse or gig on keys with my band, Paper Lanterns.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money split between those?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Library music and jingles are about two thirds of my income, the band and a bit of teaching are the rest. It's lumpy: one ad brief can pay a month's rent, then nothing for three weeks. I've got about two and a half months saved. My partner Theo is an illustrator, so we're both freelancers, which our parents find terrifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was never worried about the tools, I was worried about who owns them. Online I'd post that the boring stuff got faster and the music still needs a person with taste. Some friends would roll their eyes because I'm the one always showing them new plugins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a plateau is pretty good for me. The tools I already use make me maybe thirty percent faster, so I can take more briefs, and nobody gets replaced. If AI stops where it is now, I get a faster studio and keep my job, and I'm not going to complain about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push my output: aim for six library tracks a month instead of four. I'd put the extra money into savings until I hit four months. I'd still go to the musicians' co-op meetings about fair licensing, because the library sites keep cutting what they pay per track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the library sites cutting pay per track. Doesn't that worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but it's been happening for years, and I've made up for it with volume. I'd worry more if Theo's work dried up, but illustration is holding for now. It's an annoyance, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the extra time on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing songs for Paper Lanterns, honestly. We've got half an album and no time. If the tools give me back a day a week, that day goes to the band, not to more briefs.

say: I'd say the worry was always about **who owns** the tools.
I'd post that the boring work got faster and music still needs **human taste**.
think: A plateau is good for me: tools make me **thirty percent faster**.
Falling **library fees** are an old annoyance, not a crisis.
do: Raise output to **six library tracks** a month.
Save the extra until I reach **four months** of cushion.
Keep going to **co-op meetings** on fair licensing.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **smug** about being early to the tools.
S0.quote: If AI stops where it is now, I get a faster studio and keep my job, and I'm not going to complain about that.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **productivity gain** and sees ownership, not tools, as the threat.
Both she and Theo are **freelancers**, which shapes her eye on household risk.
She'd spend freed time on the **band**, showing what she values most.

steps.text: Produce six library tracks a month instead of four
Save extra income until four months of cushion
Attend musicians' co-op meetings on library licensing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a law that says if you train on someone's music, you pay them, and a public fund for musicians who lose work. I'd say it as someone who uses the tools every day, which I think makes people listen. I'd push the co-op to get a collective licence going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think library music is the first thing to go. If a video maker can type 'upbeat ukulele for a cooking video' and get something good for free, why license mine? Two thirds of my income is that kind of work. I'd have a couple of years before the rates collapse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd start running AI music workshops for teenagers at the youth centre on Kerr Road this spring, because I know the tools better than most teachers. I'd pitch myself to agencies as the person who directs the AI and adds the human finish, rather than competing with it. And I'd help the co-op build a catalogue we license together, with money going back to members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. My brain goes straight to plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Theo? Isn't illustration in the same boat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the bit that keeps me awake. If both our screen jobs shrink at the same time, our savings run out together. We've talked about one of us getting something steadier, and Theo's been looking at teaching art in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the tools. The companies that scraped everything and didn't pay a cent, and governments that let them. The tools are brilliant, but the companies trained them on our music for free and governments just watched.

say: I'd call for a law making AI firms **pay for training** on music.
I'd push the co-op toward a **collective licence**.
think: **Library music**, two thirds of my income, goes first.
Rates may **collapse** within a couple of years, once anyone can type a prompt for free.
do: Start **AI music workshops** for teenagers at the Kerr Road youth centre.
Pitch to agencies as the person who **directs the AI**.
Help the co-op build a **shared catalogue** paying members.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, with her mind jumping to **plans**.
S1.quote: The tools are brilliant, but the companies trained them on our music for free and governments just watched.
fieldNote: She expects her **main income** to shrink but feels she has room to steer.
The real fear is **both partners** in screen work losing income together.
She blames **companies and governments**, never the tools themselves.

steps.text: Run AI music workshops for teens at Kerr Road youth centre
Pitch agencies as an AI music director with human finish
Build a jointly licensed catalogue with the musicians' co-op
Lobby for a law making AI firms pay for music training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income. Not for musicians only, for everyone whose screen work disappears. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My composing work is gone in two years, and Theo's illustration too. That's both of us at once. Live music lasts a bit longer, until the robots in 2031, but Paper Lanterns doesn't pay rent. My partner Theo and I are both freelancers with our hands on keyboards and screens, which is exactly where this hits first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab every bit of work I could in the first year and save hard, maybe five or six hundred a month. I'd use AI tools myself to produce faster while there's still any market. I'd look at becoming a community music worker with the council, running sessions in care homes and schools, because that's people in a room. And I'd join whatever basic income campaign starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Excited about the technology and terrified for the rent, at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years before robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Live work: the band, workshops, teaching in person. Those are hands-on and social, so they last until about 2031. But they're the smaller third of my income, so I'd need to make them the whole thing, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Theo change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably move somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my mum in the suburbs, and give up the studio room. I'd hate it. But two freelancers in a city flat with no screen work is not a plan.

say: I'd say this is the moment for a **basic income** for everyone.
I'd be **organising** a campaign, not just posting.
think: My composing and Theo's illustration both **vanish** within two years.
Live work lasts to **2031**, but it's only a third of income.
do: Save **five or six hundred** a month while work lasts.
Apply to be a **community music worker** in care homes and schools.
S2.quote: My partner Theo and I are both freelancers with our hands on keyboards and screens, which is exactly where this hits first.
fieldNote: She expects **both household incomes** to collapse within two years.
Her mix of **excitement and terror** is unusual and real.
She'd move to the **people-facing** third of her work as the bridge.

steps.text: Save five to six hundred a month during the first year
Apply for council community music worker jobs in care homes
Move with Theo to a cheaper flat near her mum
Organise for a basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, which is enough to set up proper support if people move now. I'd push for the co-op licence, a fund and retraining. I'd want to say it calmly and practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Library music still goes, probably by 2029. But five years gives me time to build the workshop and community music side so it's half my income by the time composing dries up. Theo has time to move into teaching. Live work holds until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the council's community music qualification, which is evening classes. I'd start the AI workshops at the youth centre and pitch them to schools. I'd keep composing while it pays and save the surplus. I'd help the co-op license our catalogue to the AI firms on our terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can use. Like nerves before a gig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Licensing to AI firms? Doesn't that feed the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if they're going to train on music anyway, I'd rather they pay us for it. If the AI companies are going to learn from musicians anyway, the musicians' co-op should at least send them an invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make five years go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Theo and I both lost work in the same year before the new stuff was paying. Or if the council cut arts funding. That's my nightmare: being ready to switch, and the job I'm switching to gets cut.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to build support if we start now.
I'd push for the co-op licence, a fund and **retraining**.
think: Workshops and community work could be **half my income** by then, if I start now.
do: Take the council's **community music** qualification in the evenings.
Pitch **AI workshops** to schools as well as the youth centre.
License the co-op catalogue to **AI firms** on our terms.
feel: **Anxious**, but usable, like **nerves** before a gig.
S3.quote: If the AI companies are going to learn from musicians anyway, the musicians' co-op should at least send them an invoice.
fieldNote: She'd **sell to** AI firms through the co-op rather than refuse them, a pragmatic left view.
Her nightmare is **arts funding cuts** hitting the job she's moving to.
Five years turns her plan into a **steady shift** rather than a scramble.

steps.text: Complete the council's evening community music qualification
Pitch AI music workshops to local schools
License the co-op music catalogue to AI firms for payment
Save surplus composing income each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to share the gains fairly. Tax the companies, fund culture and pay people to retrain. I'd sound almost hopeful, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, which is a nice age to be doing community music, teaching and playing. Composing for libraries would fade over the decade. With ten years I could slowly turn my work toward people in rooms, and keep using the tools to make that work better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the workshops over two or three years, using AI tools to make lessons. I'd keep composing while it pays and put a fixed sum aside each month. I'd also think about having kids in a few years, once I can see what income looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy, because a decade has a way of disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would the timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With two years I'd say not a chance. With ten I'd say maybe, once the new work is steady. Whether I have a baby at thirty-one depends on whether anyone still pays for music written by a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI tools every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. I'd use them to make lessons, backing tracks and recordings for the people in my workshops. The tools were never my enemy. The question is who gets paid.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty to share the gains fairly.
I'd call for taxing firms to fund **culture and retraining**.
think: By 37 I could be doing **community music**, teaching and playing, and enjoying it.
do: Build **workshops** up over two or three years.
Keep composing and set aside a **fixed sum** monthly.
Revisit **having children** once new work is steady.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit uneasy that a **decade** goes quickly.
S4.quote: Whether I have a baby at thirty-one depends on whether anyone still pays for music written by a person.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her treat the change as a **career shift** she can steer.
**Having children** is directly tied to her income picture.
She keeps her **daily AI use** and frames the issue as payment.

steps.text: Grow AI-assisted community music workshops over three years
Set aside a fixed sum from composing each month
Decide about having a child once workshop income is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Theo and I both lose our screen work at once and there's no time to build anything else. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and a law that makes AI firms pay musicians whose work trained them. I don't hate the machines, I hate the idea that nobody who taught them gets a penny.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young people I'd teach. They're growing up thinking music comes out of a prompt box. I'd want them to know how good it feels to play a wrong note in a room full of people and laugh about it.

headlineQuote: I don't hate the machines, I hate the idea that nobody who taught them gets a penny.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old composer** of library music and jingles who also plays keys in a band.
She uses **AI tools daily** and sees ownership and payment, not the tools, as the problem.
She and partner Theo are both **freelancers** in screen work, her biggest household risk.
She's calm in the plateau, **alarmed** at two years, and steadies as warning time grows.
Her plan is to shift to **community music** workshops and license through a musicians' co-op.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Theo lose screen work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** while people retrain, and a law making AI firms **pay musicians**.
